cardio-chest-pressure.notice: New exertional pressure with a falling activity threshold deserves urgent assessment even in a young adult and even when pain stops at rest.
cardio-chest-pressure.anchor: Change in threshold, not simply rest versus exertion
cardio-chest-pressure.pivot: Compare what activity triggered the first episode with what triggers it now. Ask whether symptoms are present now before a long history.
cardio-chest-pressure.exam: Listen at four cardiac sites on skin, compare posterior lung fields, and assess circulation. A reassuring resting examination does not exclude ischemia.
cardio-chest-pressure.avoid: Calling this stable angina solely because rest relieves it; assuming young age rules out coronary disease.

cardio-febrile-cough.notice: Read temperature, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation together; fever alone does not establish pneumonia.
cardio-febrile-cough.pivot: Clarify onset, sputum, breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Ask hemoptysis and thromboembolic risks rather than assuming every cough is infectious.
cardio-febrile-cough.exam: Compare equivalent posterior lung sites, then percussion and tactile findings where the case supports them. Document the location of a focal abnormality.
cardio-febrile-cough.avoid: Writing both lungs clear after listening at one site, or omitting oxygen saturation from the supplied vitals.

cardio-orthopnea-edema.notice: Breathlessness when lying down and swelling suggest a fluid problem but do not by themselves identify its cause.
cardio-orthopnea-edema.pivot: Ask how many pillows are needed, whether breathlessness wakes the patient and how swelling or weight has changed. Clarify medications and adherence without blame.
cardio-orthopnea-edema.exam: Assess respiratory comfort, JVP, lungs, heart and peripheral edema; keep each observation distinct from the diagnosis of heart failure.
cardio-orthopnea-edema.avoid: Confusing orthopnea with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or using edema alone to prove heart failure.

cardio-palpitations.notice: A fast or irregular pulse is an observed pattern; the rhythm diagnosis still requires appropriate testing.
cardio-palpitations.pivot: Clarify sudden onset, episode duration, regularity, syncope, chest discomfort, stimulant exposure and thyroid symptoms.
cardio-palpitations.exam: Compare the reported episodes with the actual pulse and cardiac findings. A normal examination between episodes cannot exclude an intermittent arrhythmia.
cardio-palpitations.avoid: Equating an irregular sensation with confirmed atrial fibrillation or forgetting over-the-counter stimulants.

cardio-pleuritic-dyspnea.notice: Acute breathlessness with pleuritic discomfort requires attention to oxygenation and stability before routine questioning.
cardio-pleuritic-dyspnea.pivot: Ask onset, hemoptysis, leg symptoms, immobility and relevant hormonal or medication exposures. Risk factors change probability; they do not confirm a clot.
cardio-pleuritic-dyspnea.exam: Assess general respiratory status, bilateral air entry, heart and legs. Avoid treating a normal lung examination as exclusion of pulmonary embolism.
cardio-pleuritic-dyspnea.avoid: Reassuring from age or normal breath sounds while ignoring tachycardia, hypoxemia or abrupt onset.

cardio-presyncope.notice: Feeling about to faint is different from actual loss of consciousness; start by asking what happened in the patient's own words.
cardio-presyncope.pivot: Separate standing-triggered symptoms from symptoms while seated or lying, and ask actual loss of consciousness, bleeding and medication changes.
cardio-presyncope.exam: Assess circulation and a focused neurologic examination. Orthostatic measurement has its own timing and positioning requirements; do not invent the result from the history.
cardio-presyncope.avoid: Writing syncope when only presyncope was reported, or treating a planned orthostatic test as completed.

gi-diarrhea-dehydration.notice: Frequency, fluid intake and urine output help organize the immediate problem before choosing a cause.
gi-diarrhea-dehydration.pivot: Ask stool character and blood, duration, exposures, recent medications or antibiotics, vomiting and ability to drink.
gi-diarrhea-dehydration.exam: Assess general hydration clues, circulation and abdomen. Report individual findings rather than declaring a precise fluid deficit from appearance.
gi-diarrhea-dehydration.avoid: Omitting urine output or blood in stool; assuming every diarrheal illness needs antibiotics.

gi-epigastric-back-pain.notice: Severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back can involve several urgent abdominal and extra-abdominal causes.
gi-epigastric-back-pain.pivot: Clarify alcohol and medication exposure, vomiting, meal relation, chest symptoms and whether the pain is persistent. Ask before labeling pancreatitis.
gi-epigastric-back-pain.exam: Use a focused abdominal examination and cardiopulmonary assessment. Keep pancreatic inflammation as a working assessment pending appropriate tests.
gi-epigastric-back-pain.avoid: Treating back radiation as proof of pancreatitis or overlooking cardiac symptoms.

gi-epigastric-melena.notice: Black stools with upper abdominal symptoms may represent bleeding; assess current stability and faintness early.
gi-epigastric-melena.pivot: Clarify tarry versus merely dark stool, vomiting blood, dizziness, NSAID exposure and the actual dose and frequency used.
gi-epigastric-melena.exam: Assess circulation, pallor and abdomen. A proposed rectal examination is refused under the course SP rules; refusal cannot provide occult-blood or internal findings.
gi-epigastric-melena.avoid: Documenting a rectal result that was never obtained or treating improvement with acid medication as reassurance against bleeding.

gi-progressive-dysphagia.notice: Distinguish difficulty initiating a swallow from food sticking after swallowing; solids and liquids provide different clues.
gi-progressive-dysphagia.anchor: Where it sticks, what sticks, how it changes
gi-progressive-dysphagia.pivot: Ask progression, solids versus liquids, food impaction, pain on swallowing, reflux, atopy and weight change. Clarify inability to swallow saliva promptly.
gi-progressive-dysphagia.exam: Inspect the mouth and neck and assess general condition; a normal surface examination cannot establish a normal esophagus.
gi-progressive-dysphagia.avoid: Writing odynophagia when the patient describes painless sticking, or treating a future endoscopy as a current finding.

gi-right-lower-pain.notice: Right lower abdominal pain in this cohort requires pregnancy possibility to remain part of the differential without assuming pregnancy.
gi-right-lower-pain.pivot: Ask where pain began, migration, anorexia, vomiting, bowel and urinary symptoms, menstrual timing and pregnancy possibility.
gi-right-lower-pain.exam: Inspect, auscultate and then assess the abdomen with specific gentle maneuvers; explain discomfort and do not repeat provocative tests indiscriminately.
gi-right-lower-pain.avoid: Using a patient's belief that pregnancy is unlikely as a negative pregnancy test, or overlooking urinary alternatives.

gi-right-upper-pain.notice: A meal association is only the beginning: persistent pain and fever change the urgency compared with a brief resolved episode.
gi-right-upper-pain.anchor: Brief attack versus persistent inflammatory pain
gi-right-upper-pain.pivot: Ask episode duration, continuity, fever, jaundice, shoulder radiation and prior attacks. Check relevant medication exposures rather than inventing them.
gi-right-upper-pain.exam: Follow inspection, auscultation, percussion and gentle palpation. Obtain Murphy response with its specific maneuver; it is not released by clicking the abdomen.
gi-right-upper-pain.avoid: Calling all meal-related pain simple biliary colic or documenting an ultrasound result before ordering and obtaining it.

neuro-acute-focal-weakness.notice: Sudden focal weakness makes last-known-well time and immediate escalation more useful than a long routine history.
neuro-acute-focal-weakness.anchor: Last known well, deficit, emergency response
neuro-acute-focal-weakness.pivot: Clarify exact onset or last time normal, speech or vision changes, medications and whether deficits persist. Do not wait for every ROS item before activating emergency assessment.
neuro-acute-focal-weakness.exam: Assess specific mental status, cranial and limb functions and arrange glucose testing; do not equate a proposed glucose check with a result.
neuro-acute-focal-weakness.avoid: Calling an incomplete neurologic examination normal or delaying escalation while completing nonurgent checklist items.

neuro-back-bladder-redflags.notice: Back pain with new bladder dysfunction changes the encounter from routine mechanical pain to a possible neurologic emergency.
neuro-back-bladder-redflags.anchor: Bladder change, saddle symptoms, leg function
neuro-back-bladder-redflags.pivot: Clarify retention versus incontinence, onset, saddle sensory change, leg weakness, bowel changes and relevant infection or cancer history.
neuro-back-bladder-redflags.exam: Use specific lower-limb motor, sensory and reflex examination. Proposed invasive examination remains subject to the course refusal policy.
neuro-back-bladder-redflags.avoid: Assuming a bladder complaint is merely a urinary infection or using absent leg pain to dismiss urgent compression.

neuro-distal-neuropathy.notice: Distribution and time course organize numbness better than immediately naming a metabolic cause.
neuro-distal-neuropathy.pivot: Ask symmetric versus focal symptoms, progression, weakness, balance, diabetes history, nutrition, alcohol and medications.
neuro-distal-neuropathy.exam: Compare distal sensory modalities, strength and reflexes; document only modalities and regions actually examined.
neuro-distal-neuropathy.avoid: Writing sensation intact after testing one modality, or assuming diabetes explains every neuropathy.

neuro-positional-vertigo.notice: Brief triggered spinning is different from continuous dizziness, faintness or imbalance.
neuro-positional-vertigo.pivot: Clarify true spinning, duration of each spell, positional triggers, hearing changes, headache and focal neurologic symptoms.
neuro-positional-vertigo.exam: Assess relevant neurologic and ear findings and establish cervical suitability before a positional maneuver. Do not infer observed nystagmus from the patient's word dizzy.
neuro-positional-vertigo.avoid: Skipping safety screening before Dix–Hallpike or dismissing focal deficits because symptoms are positional.

neuro-recurrent-headache.notice: A recurring pattern can support migraine, but a changed pattern or neurologic red flag deserves separate attention.
neuro-recurrent-headache.pivot: Ask onset, frequency, duration, associated nausea and light sensitivity, aura, neurologic changes and analgesic frequency.
neuro-recurrent-headache.exam: Perform the specific neurologic and relevant head/neck examination; a reassuring result supports context but does not erase an concerning history.
neuro-recurrent-headache.avoid: Forgetting medication frequency or calling a new severe headache the patient's usual migraine without comparison.

neuro-thunderclap-headache.notice: Time to peak intensity is the pivotal question; an abrupt maximal headache is an urgent presentation.
neuro-thunderclap-headache.anchor: Seconds to peak changes the plan
neuro-thunderclap-headache.pivot: Clarify abruptness, onset time, exertional context, loss of consciousness, neck symptoms, fever and focal deficits.
neuro-thunderclap-headache.exam: Assess current mental status and specific neurologic findings while arranging emergency evaluation; imaging and lumbar puncture belong to future diagnostic planning unless supplied.
neuro-thunderclap-headache.avoid: Calling headache benign because the patient is young or the initial neurologic examination is normal.

renal-acute-retention.notice: Inability to void is different from low urine production; clarify the last normal void and discomfort early.
renal-acute-retention.anchor: Cannot empty versus making less urine
renal-acute-retention.pivot: Ask onset, suprapubic pressure, preceding urinary symptoms, new medications and neurologic red flags.
renal-acute-retention.exam: Assess abdominal/bladder and relevant neurologic findings. Bladder scanning and drainage are proposed clinical actions unless the simulator supplies a performed result.
renal-acute-retention.avoid: Documenting a catheter output that was never measured or overlooking medications with retention risk.

renal-colicky-flank.notice: Wave-like flank pain and radiation can suggest obstruction; fever or systemic illness changes urgency.
renal-colicky-flank.pivot: Ask onset, migration toward the groin, hematuria, vomiting, fever, urinary symptoms and previous confirmed stones.
renal-colicky-flank.exam: Assess abdomen and CVA tenderness specifically. A positive CVA finding alone does not separate stone from infection.
renal-colicky-flank.avoid: Inventing a prior stone history from an unrelated UTI answer, or ignoring fever when considering obstruction.

renal-dysuria.notice: Lower urinary symptoms need context: fever, flank pain, pregnancy possibility and genital symptoms may change the approach.
renal-dysuria.anchor: Lower tract versus upper tract or alternative
renal-dysuria.pivot: Clarify burning, frequency, urgency, hematuria, fever, flank pain, menstrual timing and relevant exposure or irritation history.
renal-dysuria.exam: Use general, abdominal and CVA examination where relevant. A urinalysis remains a proposed test until actually supplied.
renal-dysuria.avoid: Assuming all dysuria is bacterial cystitis or recording a negative pregnancy test from a reported menstrual history.

renal-flank-pain.notice: Fever with flank pain and urinary symptoms requires assessment of systemic illness and ability to tolerate fluids.
renal-flank-pain.pivot: Clarify fever and chills, onset, dysuria, vomiting, obstruction history, allergies and pregnancy possibility.
renal-flank-pain.exam: Assess perfusion, abdomen and specific CVA tenderness; the finding supports localization but does not provide a culture or identify an organism.
renal-flank-pain.avoid: Writing a culture result or assigning an organism before testing; missing allergy reaction details.

renal-luts-nocturia.notice: Frequency, urgency, nocturia and large urine volumes are distinct symptoms; separate them before choosing a cause.
renal-luts-nocturia.anchor: Frequency versus volume, pain versus urgency
renal-luts-nocturia.pivot: Ask voiding pattern, relation of discomfort to filling and emptying, fluid and caffeine intake, thirst and glycemic symptoms.
renal-luts-nocturia.exam: Assess the abdomen and relevant general findings. Use proposed urine and metabolic testing to evaluate alternatives rather than declaring them excluded.
renal-luts-nocturia.avoid: Calling frequency polyuria without a volume history or overlooking caffeine and other irritants.

renal-painless-hematuria.notice: Visible blood deserves evaluation even without pain; clarify urine appearance, clots and potential nonurinary bleeding.
renal-painless-hematuria.pivot: Ask timing within the stream, recent illness, urinary symptoms, menstrual contamination possibility and relevant risk or medication history.
renal-painless-hematuria.exam: Assess blood pressure, general condition and abdominal findings; urinary microscopy and protein are future discriminating tests unless supplied.
renal-painless-hematuria.avoid: Assuming painless blood is harmless or diagnosing a glomerular source without appropriate urine findings.
